lessons.title: Say it like a local: "Trawna"
lessons.goal: Locals squash "Toronto" into two quick beats. The second T drops after the N, and the first vowel almost disappears: "TRAW-na" or "TRAH-na".
lessons.practice: Say "To-ron-to" slowly, then faster and faster until it falls into two beats.

examples.tip: Keep "welcome to" light and let "TRAW" carry the weight.

lessons.title: Canadian raising: "out and about"
lessons.goal: Before the sounds t, s, f, k and p, the "ow" vowel starts higher, closer to "uh-oo". So "out" and "house" sound different from "loud" and "how". It is not "a boot", it is just a higher start.
lessons.practice: Say "loud" then "lout". Feel the vowel in "lout" start higher and shorter.

examples.means: Let's go out and walk around.
accepted: let's head out and about eh
come over to my house eh
come over to my house please
examples.tip: "House" starts high and short. Compare it with "how".

lessons.title: Canadian raising: "right" and "nice"
lessons.goal: The same trick for the "eye" vowel: before t, s, f, k and p it starts higher, like "uh-ee". So "write" and "ride" sound different, and "nice price" sounds very Canadian.
lessons.practice: Say "ride" then "write". The vowel in "write" starts higher and is shorter.

examples.say: The ice is so nice tonight.
examples.means: The ice rink is great tonight.
accepted: the ice is so nice tonight
the ice is so nice tonite

lessons.title: "Sorry" and the cot-caught merger
lessons.goal: Canadians say "sorry" with the vowel of "store": "SORE-y". And "cot" and "caught" sound the same here, one open "ah-aw" vowel.
lessons.practice: Say "store", then "sorry", keeping the same "or" sound.

examples.say: Sorry, I caught the wrong car.
examples.means: Sorry, I got on the wrong streetcar.
accepted: sorry i caught the wrong car
sorry i got the wrong car
sorry i caught the wrong car eh

lessons.title: The real "eh"
lessons.goal: Locals do use "eh", just not every sentence. It goes at the end, with a little rise, and asks you to agree: "Nice day, eh?" Think "right?" or "don't you think?".
lessons.practice: Say "Nice day, right?" then swap "right" for "eh", keeping the same rise.
lessons.listenFor: A short, friendly rise on "eh", at the end only.

examples.tip: Rise a little on "eh?". Keep it light.
"Out" starts high ("uh-oot"), then the friendly rise on "eh?".

lessons.title: Street names tourists get wrong
lessons.goal: Some Toronto names are not said the way they look: Spadina is "spa-DYE-na", Yonge is "young", and Etobicoke is "eh-TOE-bi-coe" with a silent K.
lessons.practice: Say each name three times, slowly and then at talking speed.

examples.means: Does this go to Spadina Avenue?

examples.say: I'm meeting you at Yonge and Bloor.
examples.means: I'll see you at the corner of Yonge Street and Bloor Street.
accepted: i'm meeting you at yonge and bloor
i'm meeting you at young and bloor
im meeting you at young and blore
i'm meeting you at yonge and blore

lessons.title: "Mans" and "the mandem"
lessons.goal: In Multicultural Toronto English "mans" can mean "I" or "me" ("mans is tired") or "that guy". "The mandem" is your group of friends. Both came to Toronto through Jamaican and Caribbean communities.
lessons.practice: Swap "I" for "mans" in a few of your own sentences.
lessons.listenFor: "Mans" said flat and sure, no question in it.

lessons.title: "Ahlie", "styll" and "bare"
lessons.goal: "Ahlie?" asks "right? for real?" at the end of a line. "Styll" at the end means "for real, though". "Bare" means "a lot" or "very". Toronto picked these up through Caribbean, Somali, South Asian and other communities who share the city.
lessons.practice: Say a line, then tag "ahlie?" (asking) or "styll" (telling) at the end.
lessons.listenFor: "Ahlie" rises like a question, "styll" lands flat.

examples.tip: Lean on "BARE COLD", then a quick "ah-lie?".

examples.say: That was a good game, styll.
examples.means: That was a good game, for real.
accepted: that was a good game styll
that was a good game still

lessons.title: "Wagwan", "say less" and "fam"
lessons.goal: "Wagwan" (from Jamaican Patois "what's going on") is hello. "Say less" means "got it, no need to explain". "Fam" is a friend.
lessons.practice: Greet three people in your head: "Wagwan, fam."

lessons.title: The Toronto street rhythm
lessons.goal: Young Torontonians often give syllables more even weight than standard Canadian English, and "th" can become "t" or "d": "ting" for "thing", "dem" for "them". Keep it relaxed and confident, never rushed.
lessons.practice: Tap the table once per syllable and keep the taps even.
lessons.listenFor: Even beats; "ting", "dem" with a clean T and D.

examples.tip: "Ting" with a clean T, even beats.

ok.text: Close, bud. Once more, nice and relaxed.

bad.text: Hmm, not quite. Listen again and copy the tune, eh.
